video_title: Decagon’s Playbook for Building Enterprise AI Applications
gist: Decagon's two co-founders (Jesse and Asha) explain how their customer-service/concierge agent company moved 90% of its production workflow onto fine-tuned open-source models for latency, why they argue the cost-vs-intelligence trade-off is false, and why the application layer keeps a moat even against AGI-class labs. They also detail the economics of forward-deployed engineering (productize or become consulting), a head-to-head win against Sierra on 'glass box vs black box' iteration speed (7 new journeys in a month vs 3 in a year), and a Jevons-paradox view that cheaper support expands support volume rather than cutting headcount.

themes.theme: Open-source model stack and Decagon Labs

insights.claim: Decagon now runs roughly 90% of its production agent workflow on fine-tuned open-source models, a shift begun about a year ago primarily to cut latency for its voice agent, with the remaining ~10% still on closed frontier models for new products and experiments.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: A reference point for how fast a leading AI application company shifts inference off frontier APIs: production scale plus voice latency, not cost, is the trigger, which caps frontier-lab revenue per mature use case.
insights.quote: So today 90% of our workflow is on open source

insights.claim: Fine-tuning a smaller, 'dumber' open-source model on one narrow task makes it outperform large state-of-the-art frontier models on that task while also being cheaper and faster, so the widely debated cost-versus-intelligence trade-off is a false trade-off.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: If specialization dominates generality on narrow production tasks, per-token frontier pricing power erodes for any workload that stabilizes, and post-training tooling/talent becomes the scarce asset.
insights.quote: So we end up getting all three things. It is better at the toss. It is cheaper and it is faster.

insights.claim: Decagon evaluates every model along exactly three dimensions — cost, intelligence and latency — and deliberately sacrifices general intelligence to sit at the frontier of latency when the agent only has to do one narrow task.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: A reusable screen for evaluating any agent company's model strategy: ask which of the three axes they are optimizing and whether the use case actually needs frontier intelligence.
insights.quote: every model you can kind of evaluate along three dimensions. It's you know cost intelligence and latency

insights.claim: A single Decagon conversation is decomposed into many small sub-tasks — detecting the customer's topic, detecting whether the caller is a bad actor, and so on — and none of those sub-tasks individually requires the full intelligence of a large model.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Task decomposition is the mechanism that makes small-model substitution work; companies that never decompose their agent stay structurally dependent on frontier pricing.

insights.claim: Decagon still uses frontier models for broad, open-ended work such as Duet Autopilot, which reviews a million past conversations, finds trends, generates variants of the primary conversational model and tests which variants perform better.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Frontier demand migrates from the serving path to the meta/optimization path — watch for 'agents that improve agents' as the new durable frontier-token workload.

insights.claim: The hard part of adopting open-source models is not the decision but the data and the evals: public eval sets are useless for a specific agent task, so Decagon generates its own benchmarks and funds a deliberately expensive internal research team.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Eval infrastructure, not model weights, is the real barrier to enterprise open-source adoption — a bullish signal for eval/benchmark tooling and for incumbents who already built it.

insights.claim: Despite the open-source hype, the share of enterprise inference running on open-source models is currently going down, because enterprises keep spinning up brand-new use cases and always start those on frontier APIs.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Directly against the consensus 'open source is taking share' narrative; frontier-lab enterprise revenue is protected as long as new use-case creation outruns use-case maturation.
insights.quote: the sort of share of of open source inference is actually going down right now because people are spinning up all these new use cases

insights.claim: Once a use case is solidified and in production at scale, it is strictly better to move it to open-source models for latency and cost, so enterprises are heavily incentivized to migrate — but that migration will be slow because of model risk governance, security review and the limited number of use cases an enterprise can run at once.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Frames the timing of the open-source share shift: real but slower than Twitter expects, with governance throughput as the binding constraint to watch.

insights.claim: Decagon Labs was built as a 'model factory' whose purpose is to compress the time between a new model being released and a fine-tuned, task-specific version coming out the other end, because Decagon constantly trains net-new models and deprecates old ones as the open-source and closed frontiers advance.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Model post-training is being treated as a continuous pipeline, not a project — the durable capability is release-to-production cycle time, which is a defensible operating metric to underwrite.
insights.quote: Dagon Labs is in a way a model factory of sorts

insights.claim: Decagon's in-house/outsource rule is that anything tightly coupled to its own use case gets built internally — including training infrastructure and evals measured on end-to-end customer outcomes rather than loss curves or single-task scores — while commodity work like labeled data and measuring dataset diversity is bought from vendors.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Bounds the addressable market for the RL-as-a-service and eval-vendor ecosystem: data labeling and diversity tooling sells, use-case-coupled training/eval infra does not.

insights.claim: Decagon does not optimize for token cost: latency and accuracy are the driving factors and cost falls out as a free side benefit, and as a growth-stage company growth outranks cost discipline because customers only judge how well the agent performs.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Gross-margin anxiety about AI apps may be premature for category leaders; the metric that matters at this stage is per-conversation quality, not per-conversation cost.

insights.claim: The number of tokens Decagon consumes per conversation has gone UP over time, because it deliberately makes more model calls to add quality checks and parallelize work — the opposite of the assumed cost-deflation path.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Bullish for inference demand: falling per-token prices are being absorbed by more calls per unit of work, so token volume growth can outrun price declines.

insights.claim: Decagon prices and reasons in 'unit of output' terms — the conversation — because customers care about the conversation's quality and do not care how many tokens or dollars it consumed.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Outcome-priced AI applications can decouple pricing from token cost, which is what lets margins expand later once cost optimization becomes the priority.

insights.claim: The tokenomics debate is really a frontier-model-only problem: it matters intensely if you run your whole business on frontier APIs, but once a company knows how to decompose a problem and build, train and deploy its own models quickly, the cost question becomes far less pressing.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Use it as a diligence question: a company loudly worried about tokenomics is signaling it has not yet built post-training capability.

themes.theme: Application layer's durable moat against the labs

insights.claim: A common misconception is that fine-tuning customizes an agent per customer; in fact most of Decagon's fine-tuning customizes for the use case (customer service behaviors such as selecting support topics), which is economical for a company that does only that across many customers but not for a single enterprise's research team.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Explains the structural reason a Fortune 100 buys the vertical app rather than building on a lab — use-case-level post-training amortizes only across many customers.
insights.quote: In fact, most of the fine tetuning we do is like customizing it for our use case, like the customer service use case.

insights.claim: A customer's own procedures must be taught to the agent in context rather than by fine-tuning, because fine-tuned procedures would have to be reversed every time the business changes them — and iterating on that business logic is continuous engineering effort the enterprise would own forever if it built in-house.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Identifies the recurring cost that pushes DIY enterprise agent projects back toward vendors: post-launch business-logic churn, not the initial build.

insights.claim: Capturing business logic — for example handling a caller whose flight was cancelled and who needs to rebook three people at once — has nothing to do with the models and must live in the application layer's software stack.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: The clearest statement of where value accrues if models commoditize: the encoding, testing and governance of business process, not the reasoning engine.

insights.claim: Even assuming a perfect, mistake-free model, making it deployable inside an enterprise requires software the labs don't provide: guardrails defining what the agent can and cannot do, collaboration for hundreds of internal experts, regulatory-line testing, extraction of insights from millions of conversations, and integration with legacy systems — and that is Decagon's moat for the next few years, with commoditization risk deferred roughly three years out.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: The explicit moat claim to test: if agents can build deployment scaffolding on the fly within ~3 years, vertical app valuations rest on distribution and data instead.

insights.claim: AGI will not end software, because human beings are effectively AGI and still need databases and CRMs — AGI agents will likewise need somewhere to store work and pull information from — though a class of SaaS built solely for people to do work will face heat.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: A framework for sorting SaaS shorts from survivors: seat-priced human-workflow tools are exposed, systems of record that agents must write to are not.
insights.quote: I think even once you have AGI all our AGI agents are going to need somewhere to store work and pull information from and reason about things.

insights.claim: The app-versus-infrastructure split is converging in both directions — labs build applications to show enterprise ROI while application companies build their own models to squeeze performance, latency and cost — and long-term, application-layer companies may simply become labs for specific verticals whose primary product is task-specific models.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Predicts blurring category lines: expect vertical 'agent labs' as an emerging asset class and lab-built vertical apps as a competitive overhang.
insights.quote: maybe in the long term application layer companies just become labs for specific verticals

insights.claim: Forward-deployed engineers are newly necessary for early-stage AI companies because nobody knows the workflows yet — unlike a SaaS product five years ago where user intent was well explored, the FDE embeds with the customer to learn the workflow at the same time the customer does.
insights.speaker: Decagon co-founder
insights.so_what: Gives a time-bound justification for FDE-heavy cost structures: acceptable during workflow discovery, a warning sign once the workflow is known.

insights.claim: The current Silicon Valley enthusiasm for hiring large forward-deployed-engineer teams is a trap: once you know the workflow you should productize it, and if you cannot productize it you are just building a glorified consulting shop with no tech-company scaling properties.
insights.speaker: Decagon co-founder
insights.so_what: A screen for AI application diligence: ask what share of FDE output lands in core product versus one-off customer builds before underwriting software multiples.
insights.quote: And if you can't do that, then you're just building a glorified consulting truck.

insights.claim: Palantir's forward-deployed model is largely non-replicable because very few companies can close massive deals off the bat that make the effort worthwhile, and companies pursuing 'we'll do any AI use case for you' will eventually have to find a scalable product or accept being a modern Accenture.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder, former deployment strategist)
insights.so_what: Direct pushback on the most-copied AI GTM playbook; the term 'FDE' is used loosely and conflating consulting with product is how AI startups end up at services multiples.

insights.claim: Decagon's forward-deployed engineers build core product rather than one-off customer work, with the explicit rule that the output is contributed back so the next ten customers who ask for the same thing get it for free.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable operating standard that separates scalable AI application companies from disguised services businesses.

insights.claim: Decagon's agent PMs productize the deployment process itself, walking very large enterprises through changing their internal processes to a state where AI agents do much of the work — so 'product improvement' includes process artifacts, not just software.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Repeatable change-management IP is an underrated moat component in enterprise AI and shows up as faster go-live, not as a feature list.

insights.claim: Decagon describes itself as simultaneously product-led and sales-led: the roadmap is informed by sales rather than invented internally, but every learning from customer-facing work must compile into the core product or the company cannot scale, with the stated bet that the winner in the space will be the most product-driven.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: The operating discipline behind fast enterprise growth without services drag — and the failure mode to watch if the company starts chasing bespoke use cases for bigger contracts.
insights.quote: we really view ourselves uh in our core it's a it's a productled company

themes.theme: Duet and AOPs: productizing the agent build loop

insights.claim: Agent operating procedures (AOPs) — Decagon's own format for teaching an AI how to do things in plain text — were themselves a productization of forward-deployed toil, replacing the earlier requirement that every procedure be written in code.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Shows the productization flywheel concretely: each FDE bottleneck becomes a product primitive, which is what converts services cost into gross margin.

insights.claim: Duet is a second, much bigger and slower agent whose job is to build and operate the customer-facing agent: given only raw transcripts and documentation it writes the AOPs, the tool integrations into customer systems, and the tests and simulations, then monitors production conversations and flags the topics being handled poorly.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: The clearest example of agents replacing the implementation labor inside an AI vendor — the mechanism by which AI application gross margins can improve over time.
insights.quote: instead of us having to write these AOPs and write these integrations and tools into their systems and write these tests and monitor the conversations, do just does all of that

insights.claim: Duet was impossible when Decagon was founded and only became feasible as reasoning models improved — models that the frontier labs built mainly for coding agents turned out to generalize to tasks they were never trained on, like writing operating procedures and tests.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Coding-optimized reasoning progress spills over into non-coding enterprise automation, so frontier model releases are a direct catalyst for application-layer margin structure.

insights.claim: Duet Autopilot was a second productization step: after Duet automated the initial build, the remaining forward-deployed time went into post-launch iteration — reviewing conversations and figuring out improvements — so that loop was turned into a product too.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Signals where the next productization target is in any agent business: whichever human loop still scales linearly with customers.

themes.theme: Enterprise GTM and the Sierra head-to-head

insights.claim: Decagon's most recent customer switched off Sierra, citing a deployment model that ran mostly through forward-deployed engineers and felt like a black box: everything from building new journeys to understanding conversations required going through the FDEs, which created drag once those FDEs were staffed elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: A specific competitive win mechanism in the AI customer-service category: FDE-mediated delivery becomes a churn vector once the customer wants to iterate independently.

insights.claim: That switching customer built about three new agent journeys over a year on the incumbent, then roughly seven new journeys in about a month on Decagon — the quantitative case for a 'glass box' productized approach over a 'black box' services approach.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Journeys-shipped-per-month is a usable competitive KPI for agent platforms and a leading indicator of expansion revenue.
insights.quote: within a basically a month they spun up like seven new journeys on Ducky

insights.claim: Decagon wins big regulated deals partly by mapping the go-live journey in granular detail during the sales process — walking the buyer through their likely model risk process, testing plan, initial rollout, issue remediation and prevention — because enterprises ask not only whether the product works but whether they can actually get it live.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Deployment-path credibility, not feature parity, is what compresses enterprise AI sales cycles — a differentiator most tech vendors overlook.
insights.quote: we can walk them through in very granular detail, how we go from this first meeting today to going live at 100%

insights.claim: One Decagon co-founder estimates spending roughly 80% of his time on sales, largely to be the force pushing both his own team and the customer partnership to move faster, and to invent process and product configurations that a sales team cannot own.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Benchmark for founder-led enterprise AI GTM: deal velocity at this stage is a founder-time input, which is also a scaling risk as the company grows.
insights.quote: Uh I probably spend most of my time like 80% maybe.

insights.claim: With the world's largest banks, airlines and telcos, Decagon deliberately piecemeals projects — picking one or two top use cases to get a win rather than deploying across every surface and use case at once — because no amount of urgency removes the inertia of a massive organization.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Land-and-expand at the use-case level is the practical path into regulated giants; expect initial contract sizes to understate account potential.

insights.claim: Sales cycles in AI customer service are unusually fast because the vendor does not have to convince buyers to invest in the category at all — the conversation is only about which approach to partner with — and Decagon's founders learned enterprise selling on the job having never sold to enterprises before.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Category-level demand pull is doing part of the selling, which flatters current AI application growth rates and makes them harder to attribute to durable execution.

insights.claim: Decagon's early sales team was built from non-traditional profiles — some candidates cold applied after watching the company from inside the space, plus a cohort of Ivy League athletes — and the whole company operates on the premise that everything starts with sales and propagates back into product.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Hiring pattern worth copying for fast-moving categories: domain-adjacent cold inbound and high-intensity generalists over credentialed enterprise reps.

insights.claim: Founder time spent with prospects and existing customers is treated as the model-capability feedback loop: because model capabilities change constantly, customers are the fastest signal on what competitors or new models can now do that Decagon does not yet do.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: In fast-moving AI markets, customer conversations substitute for roadmap planning — a reason founder-led sales persists longer than in classic SaaS.

insights.claim: AI companies are being pulled internationally far earlier than classic SaaS — Decagon has opened Australia, London and New York offices and brought in former VMware CEO Raghu Raghuram to help build international capability — driven by top-down board and CEO pressure to adopt AI and by AI collapsing the language-localization barrier, with data residency requirements and better-informed local competitors as the counterweights.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Earlier international expansion changes the capital and hiring profile of AI application companies and opens a window for regional AI agent competitors.
insights.quote: and then the other trend is that language is a lot easier with AI

themes.theme: From support wedge to AI concierge

insights.claim: Decagon's long-term vision is that an AI agent becomes the front door of a business or brand, handling every customer interaction whether reactive or proactive — with customer service being just one large pillar of inbound interactions.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Defines a much larger TAM than support deflection — the interaction layer of the business — and puts Decagon on a collision path with sales, marketing and ops software.
insights.quote: an AI agent should just be the front door of your business or your brand and every interaction whether it's like reactive or proactive with a customer uh should be handled by by AI

insights.claim: Decagon started in customer support for two reasons: it was one of the biggest challenges its early customers faced, and it was the outer limit of what models could actually do at the time.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Model capability, not market choice, set the initial wedge — so capability improvements mechanically expand the product surface a vendor can sell.

insights.claim: Decagon deliberately built not an agent that does customer support well but an agent that follows business process well, which is why inbound sales qualification and operational workflows are the same underlying product.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: The architectural decision that enables land-and-expand beyond support; it is also the claim to test when assessing whether Decagon can win non-support budgets.
insights.quote: the thing that we built and we kind of built this intentionally from the start was not an agent that does customer support well but rather an agent that follows business process well

insights.claim: The specific model capability that unlocked the expansion beyond support was instruction following: earlier models needed very tight, specific guidance, while newer models can be given broad instructions and trusted to interpret and fill gaps like a human, which is required for open-ended sales discovery conversations that bob and weave.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: A concrete capability metric to track when forecasting which enterprise workflows become automatable next: tolerance for loose instructions, not raw benchmark IQ.
insights.quote: It is specifically the ability to follow instructions.

insights.claim: Expansion is already happening inside the base: one customer that went live for support asked Decagon to handle inbound sales — answering questions, doing discovery and routing large deals to enterprise reps — and another uses it for operational workflows including proactive outreach when issues appear on an account.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Evidence of net revenue retention mechanics: the support deployment builds the product and brand knowledge that makes adjacent use cases an easy upsell.

insights.claim: A detailed 12-month product roadmap is not realistic in today's AI market; at most you hold a few themes, and if you know the theme you should build it immediately because building is now so fast.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Planning-horizon collapse is itself a competitive variable — vendors with annual roadmap cycles lose to those shipping against live customer signal.
insights.quote: in today's AI world it's very difficult to have like a a 12-month road map to a tea

insights.claim: The economic thesis behind the concierge framing is democratizing service levels: a customer spending $100,000 a year gets fully personalized treatment today while a customer spending $10 cannot, purely because the unit economics do not support it — and delivering that experience for around ten cents makes it economical for everyone.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Frames the market as demand creation rather than cost substitution, which supports the volume-expansion (rather than headcount-reduction) revenue case.
insights.quote: It is not a lack of desire to do this for their customers. It is just that the unit economics don't support that.

insights.claim: Decagon built horizontally on the thesis that winners in the customer-interaction space will be horizontal — citing Salesforce and Zendesk as historically horizontal winners — because scale plus a robust, deep product beats vertical-specific features, with consolidation expected across geographies, verticals and market segments.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Bearish read on pure-vertical AI customer-service startups: they may find niches but face consolidation rather than standalone survival.
insights.quote: our view the reason why we've kind of built so horizontally is that we believe that in our space the winners are going to be horizontal

insights.claim: CRM is not disintermediated by AI concierges and could actually do well: agents still need somewhere to write customer information, and in a world where agents rather than humans use the interfaces, the CRM's value as source of truth persists even without graphical UIs — and Decagon has zero desire to build one.
insights.speaker: Jesse and Asha (Decagon co-founders)
insights.so_what: A bullish-on-systems-of-record take from the agent layer itself: usage may shift from seats to agent API calls, which changes CRM pricing models more than CRM demand.
insights.quote: we have zero desire to build a CRM because we think there's so much to do in the agentic layer

insights.claim: Latent demand for customer support exceeds supply, so when the cost of support drops by around 30% most Decagon customers do not lay off 60% of the team — they buy more support to improve retention, reduce churn and speed activation.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: If support is demand-elastic, AI agent revenue grows with expanded volume rather than being capped by the incumbent support wage bill.
insights.quote: if our cost of doing customer support drops by 30%. Most of them are not just immediately saying, okay, now what I will do is, you know, let go of 60% of my team.

insights.claim: A Decagon customer running roughly 50,000 support inquiries a month discovered after deploying AI that customers had far more problems than measured, and responded by putting support on every page, making it prominent where users get stuck, and opening immediate support to free users rather than only paying users.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: A concrete Jevons-paradox datapoint: automation expanded the surface area of the workload, meaning per-customer AI conversation volume can grow far beyond the pre-AI ticket baseline.

insights.claim: Outcomes for outsourced BPO providers vary by customer situation: some use their BPOs much less or drop them, while others are not in cost-cutting mode and instead hold operations headcount flat through rapid business growth or redeploy people to revenue-generating work.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: BPO disruption is real but uneven — the near-term hit shows up as flat-to-declining incremental seat growth rather than mass contract cancellation.

insights.claim: The adoption sequence in conversational AI is cost-cutting use cases first because they are easy, then revenue-generating use cases delivered through the same conversational interface — which Decagon flags as a big area for itself as the AI matures.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Watch for the pricing shift from cost-savings ROI to revenue share, which would materially raise the ceiling on agent contract values.

insights.claim: Decagon's binding bottleneck is hiring rather than model capability — the company describes itself as a voracious token consumer with very large token bills — and AI agents cannot yet be substituted because they can execute specific steps but cannot decide what to build, what to exclude, or judge whether something is done.
insights.speaker: Asha and Jesse (Decagon co-founders)
insights.so_what: Taste and prioritization are the remaining human bottleneck inside even the most AI-native companies — a boundary condition for the 'agents replace product teams' thesis.
insights.quote: we are voracious consumers of tokens but we would always love more great people

insights.claim: The one-person-unicorn narrative is contradicted by the fact that AI coding startups — presumably the most sophisticated users of these models — are hiring aggressively, because when everyone gains the same leverage each company reinvests it into building three times as much rather than shrinking headcount.
insights.speaker: Asha (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: Competitive dynamics, not productivity math, determine AI-era headcount — so software engineering employment forecasts based on per-engineer output gains are likely wrong.
insights.quote: the AI coding startups are hiring like crazy

insights.claim: The view offered on labor is that AI will kill jobs but not careers: high-volume, mundane, click-through work should not be done by humans, while there is a near-infinite amount of higher-value customer work people can shift into.
insights.speaker: Jesse (Decagon co-founder)
insights.so_what: The narrative framing AI vendors will use with enterprise buyers and regulators — useful for anticipating how support automation gets sold politically inside large employers.
insights.quote: AI will uh kill jobs but not careers in a way because like those jobs that are being done currently should not be done by humans
